We were really lucky to find tickets leaving from Canada (Ottawa) to Hong Kong for 600$. We would be in China from September 2 to the 16. Any DOs and DON'Ts?
Just bought tickets to China (Hong Kong). What should I do for 2 weeks in September?

• Do take a walk around the outdoor markets. They have a street that's just for fish, one for flowers, one for birds, another for women's clothes, and a few more.
  • Take a harbor tour. It's cheap and scenic.
  • Hong Kong Disney is fantastic, even if you've seen the other Disney parks. Stay for the light parade.
  • Go to the top of HK and take in the great views.

  • Visit the SoHo district with the escalators for solid nightlife (if a bit westernish).

  • Don't take offense if someone cuts in front of you in line or reaches over the register and places their stuff down on the counter despite you being next. To the mainland Chinese, if you're not budging, you're not in line. It's just how they do it.

  • Don't be surprised if people cuddle you in close quarters. Personal space is very different there.
  • Don't expect any VPN or your favorite websites to work. The firewall and govt internet crackdown is very real.
Would you recommend going up on the peak to get a good view, or is it most likely going to be covered by smog and not worth it?

You may judge for yourself. I'm not sure if it's smog or just the way the mountains trap the moisture from the sea (similar to Portland). But it's a neat ride up a funicular and there's walking trails around the peaks. HK is a very vertical city in every sense, so we appreciated going above it.

If you're interested at all in flashy casinos and/or a blending of European and Asian cultures, you could also hop the ferry over to Macau. I haven't been personally, but many of my students have raved about it. There's some very tasty Portuguese cuisine to be had, and a good amount of history too, if you can look past all the gambling.

I think the main problem is sorting/routing. It's cheaper to have few huge heavily automated facilities and route everything to/from them than to distribute the problem.

There would also be fewer trucks/planes as well, traveling less distance, I'm sure. Let's take six cities, if my math is right there are 240 routes between them all (one in each direction so 2x(5x4x3x2)). If you through a single hub then you only have 10, so you save right away on the number of planes/trucks/pilots, etc. You could argue that you could hop between nodes (cities) to reduce the # of routes and have shorter average travel distances for each package, but remember that each hop requires any package to be unloaded/sorted/reloaded and that adds delays.
